title: Imports, the module cache, and avoiding startup surprises
masterChecklist: Imports, import forms, import-time effects, module cache, sys.path, dir, __name__
User modules, packages, __init__.py, relative imports, namespace packages, public API design
whyItMatters: An import runs a module's top-level code the first time it is loaded. If that code opens files, starts work, or changes configuration, a harmless-looking import can make tests and command-line tools unpredictable.
simpleExplanation: Python finds a module, creates a module object, executes its top-level statements, then stores that object in sys.modules. Later imports normally reuse the cached object. The name __name__ is '__main__' only for the file started directly, making it a safe place for a program entry point.
mentalModel: Importing a module is like opening a workshop for the first time: its setup happens once, then later visitors use the existing workshop rather than building another one.
outcomes: Explain that importing executes top-level module code once per process in the usual case.
Put command-line-only work behind an if __name__ == '__main__' guard.
Distinguish import package from from package import name.
Avoid relying on import order as hidden application setup.

realWorldExample.scenario: A course-report package exposes formatting helpers and also has a command-line report command.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: If the report is generated at module import time, a test that merely imports the helper can create files or print noisy output.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Keep definitions import-safe and call main() only under the __main__ guard. Make configuration explicit at the program boundary.

explanation: format_title is defined without doing work just because another module imports it.
main contains the action appropriate when this file is deliberately started as a program.
The guard is true for python report.py and false when another file imports report.
This design lets tests import and call format_title without triggering output.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Create another file that imports report and calls format_title. Confirm that it receives no unexpected report output during import.

procedure: Keep constants, classes, and function definitions safe to import.
Put command-line parsing and side effects in main().
Call main only under the __name__ guard.
Use clear absolute imports in an application; use relative imports deliberately inside a package.
Treat module-level mutable state as process-wide state and avoid using it as hidden configuration.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing print, file writes, or network setup at module top level.
commonMistakes.why: Every first import triggers it and tests cannot import the module cleanly.
commonMistakes.avoid: Move action into a function and call it from a guarded main entry point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming an import re-runs a module to reset its state.
commonMistakes.why: The module cache normally reuses the already-created object.
commonMistakes.avoid: Pass explicit state or construct a new object for each test or run.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using from module import * in application code.
commonMistakes.why: It obscures where names came from and risks accidental collisions.
commonMistakes.avoid: Import the module or explicitly named public items.

lab.title: Make a report helper safe to import
lab.safety: Uses only local text and console output.
guidedSteps: Keep format_title outside the guard so other modules can import it.
Run this file directly, then import it from another file to compare behavior.
checks: Calls main only inside the guard.
Does not depend on import order for configuration.
hints: Use a double underscore on both sides of name.
The final line should be indented under the if statement.
lab.solutionExplanation: The helper remains available when another file imports this module. The printing action happens only when this file is deliberately launched as the program entry point.
challenges: Predict whether two imports of the same module normally run its top-level code twice.
Find the bug in a module that creates a database connection before any function definition.
Experiment: print __name__ from a directly run file and from an imported file.

projectConnection.milestone: Separate import-safe report functions from one main command that reads local input and prints a report.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Tests can import every helper without creating output or files, while running the entry file directly invokes main once.

assessment.question: What normally happens during the first import of a module?
assessment.answer: Python executes its top-level code and stores the resulting module object in a cache.
assessment.explanation: Later ordinary imports usually reuse the cached module object.

assessment.question: Why use if __name__ == '__main__'?
assessment.answer: To run program-entry behavior only when that file starts directly.
assessment.explanation: Imported helpers remain safe to reuse and test.

assessment.question: Why avoid import *?
assessment.answer: It hides name origins and can overwrite names unexpectedly.
assessment.explanation: Explicit imports make dependencies and public APIs clearer.
